1.1: The compar:IA website provides easy and free access to a wide variety of conversational AI models, raising public awareness of the various challenges of generative AI: diversity, bias, and environmental impact. Furthermore, the datasets of questions and preferences compiled are shared as open source under the MIT/Etalab 2.0 license.
1.2: The target users of the Compar:IA service were identified by conducting user interviews and a preliminary phase of needs investigation.
1.3: Thus, all citizens are concerned as potential users, but particularly teachers, pupils, students, workshop facilitators, AI trainers, as well as researchers (computer science, AI, humanities and social sciences) and companies interested in analyzing or using open-source shared datasets. Accordingly, the digital service meets their needs through the following features: testing and comparing models for free, and using open-source shared data.
1.4: The compar:IA service is part of an eco-design approach aimed at reducing environmental impacts. To this end, this declaration was drafted within the framework of the implementation of the General Eco-design Framework for Digital Services (RGESN, version 2024). The RGESN, produced by Arcep and Arcom, in collaboration with ADEME, DINUM, CNIL, and Inria, is available on the Arcep website.
1.title: Purpose of this service

2.1: Eco-design of digital services is an approach aimed at reducing and limiting the environmental impacts of a service from its design phase and throughout its life cycle.
Designing more sustainable digital services to extend the lifespan of devices;
2.2: Promote an approach based on environmental sobriety in response to user attention capture strategies, in line with international environmental objectives;
2.3: Reduce the IT resources used, optimize data traffic and the use of digital infrastructure;
2.4: Increase the level of transparency on the environmental footprint of the digital service.
2.title: Its implementation pursues four main objectives:

3.1: Limit the size of a page
3.2: Limit the complexity of a page
3.3: Limit the number of server requests
3.4: Limit the energy consumption required to host the service
3.title: In practical terms, eco-design translates into a set of best practices to be followed before, during, and after the creation or improvement of a service, enabling, in particular:

2.4: This is a process of continuous and collective improvement.
2.title: What is eco-design?

1.1: Simplifying the user experience: navigation paths are optimized and centered around the essential features of the Compar:IA service (arena of models to test, datasets, ranking) with regular user testing.
1.2: Raising awareness among users about the ecological footprint of the service: highlighting energy impact indicators on questions asked to AI; promoting "frugal" uses, with a mode dedicated to querying "small" conversational AI models whose environmental impact is smaller.
1.3: Use of State Design System (DSFR) interface components: they are accessible and their footprint is minimal.
1.4: The most intuitive navigation possible to reduce the time spent finding information.
1.5: Mobile-first design: all content is viewable on mobile devices. The site adapts to all screen sizes.
1.6: Exclusion of video integration on the site.
1.title: The main challenge is to ensure that the compar:IA service works on the oldest possible user devices, under varying connectivity conditions. Several measures were implemented during the design phase, including:

3.title: Strategy implemented and objectives regarding the reduction or limitation of environmental impacts

4.1: The self-assessment, conducted between May and October 2025 by the product team (two people were responsible for reviewing and validating all criteria), covered all pages of the site. The tools used to evaluate certain technical indicators were the browser's developer tools' "network" inspector, the Green IT Analysis extension, and the EcoIndex tool.
4.title: RGESN Diagnosis

1.1: Progress score in the implementation of the RGESN, as of 10/12/2025: 89%
1.title: The self-diagnosis gives a compliance rate with the RGESN (general ecodesign reference) of 89%.

5.2: The digital service compar:IA aims to improve this progress score to reach 95% by 2027.
5.title: Score in the implementation of the framework

6.1: The site is designed to be accessible for any mobile device dating from 2017 or later.
6.2: Minimum connection required for comfortable access and use of the service: 3G on mobile and 512 Kbps on fixed connection.
6.3: The site is designed for different screen sizes (minimum 320 pixels wide).
6.4: The site is not accessible via the Internet Explorer browser.
6.title: Minimum requirements to access the site

7.1: Design the service with a design review and a code review, one of the objectives of which is to reduce the environmental impacts of each feature (criterion 2.1)
7.2: Implement data retention periods for the purpose of deletion or archiving: regular deletion of logs in the "S3" file server and the database (Postgres) in particular.

3.1: Maximum number of server requests per screen: 40
3.2: Maximum resource size per screen: 600 KB
3.title: To adhere to a maximum weight and a limit on the number of requests per screen (criterion 6.1):

7.4: Convert the illustrations to WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL or a more efficient image format for raster images (criterion 5.1).
7.5: Allow the possibility to interrupt inference (loading of responses) during model comparison.
7.6: EcoIndex analysis scores demonstrate a significant discrepancy in impact measurements, with some pages receiving scores of up to E or F (relatively large page weight, complexity, and number of requests); the challenge now is to understand these results more precisely on a case-by-case basis, despite the good practices implemented, in order to identify further improvements.
7.desc: Several improvements have been or are still being identified, including:
7.title: Improvements identified

8.1: Stylesheet trimmed from 3.27 MB to 1.46 MB, which is 239 KB less after compression on each page: the service no longer carries the design system's 1,047 icons, only the twenty-five it uses.
8.2: Removal of 344 KB of public files that no page called for.
8.3: Session recording stopped: it watched mouse movements and page changes for the whole visit, producing recordings nobody looked at. Page counting is kept.
8.4: Measured on 13 August 2026 on the chat screen: 111 requests and 1,152 KB. The service is still above the limits it set itself above, 40 requests and 600 KB per screen. The largest remaining item is the translation file, which carries all five languages on every page.

dense.desc: Dense architecture refers to a type of neural network in which each neuron in one layer is connected to all neurons in the next layer. This allows all parameters in the layer to contribute to the output calculation.
dense.name: Dense

matformer.desc: Imagine **Russian dolls** (matryoshkas → matryoshka transformer → Matformer): each block contains several **nested sub-models** of increasing size, sharing the same parameters. This allows, for each request, to select a model of adapted capacity, according to the available memory or latency, without needing to re-train different models.
matformer.name: Matformer

moe.desc: The Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture uses a routing mechanism to activate, depending on the input, only certain specialized subsets (“experts”) of the neural network. This allows for the construction of very large models while keeping computational costs low, because only a part of the network is used at each step.
moe.name: MoE

na.name: N/A

energy.tooltip: EcoLogits 0.10.2 estimate for generating 1 million output tokens. The calculation uses the total number of parameters and, for mixture of experts (MoE) models, the number of active parameters. Assumptions: data centre energy efficiency (PUE) of 1.2, latency not given, and the median value when the result is a range. Thresholds: A < 100 Wh; B < 300 Wh; C < 1,000 Wh; D < 3,000 Wh; E < 10,000 Wh; F ≥ 10,000 Wh. This is not a measurement from the provider: the actual hardware, the quantization, the length of the inputs and the latency can all change the consumption.

energy.desc: This graph represents the satisfaction score (Bradley Terry score) for each model as a function of the estimated average energy consumption per 1000 tokens. Energy consumption is estimated using the Ecologits methodology and is based on two parameters: the size of the models (number of parameters) and their architecture. For proprietary models, this information is either not provided or only partially available. Therefore, they are excluded from the graph below.

list.2: At the top left are the models that are popular and consume less energy compared to other models.
list.3: Beyond size, architecture has an impact on the average energy consumption of models: for example, with a similar size, the Llama 3 405B model (dense architecture, 405 billion parameters) consumes 10 times more energy on average than the GLM 4.5 model (MOE architecture, 355 billion parameters and 32 billion active parameters).

descs.1: The estimation of energy consumption for model inference relies on the Ecologits methodology, which takes into account the size and architecture of the models. However, this information is not made public by model developers for proprietary models.
descs.2: We have therefore decided not to integrate proprietary models into the graph until the information contributing used for the calculation of energy consumption is transparent.

2.title: Why are the proprietary models not displayed on the graph?

descs.1: The arena uses the methodology developed by Ecologits (GenAI Impact) to provide an estimate of the energy footprint associated with inferring conversational generative AI models. This estimate allows users to compare the environmental impact of different AI models for the same query. This transparency is essential to encourage the development and adoption of more eco-friendly AI models.
descs.2: Ecologits applies the principles of life cycle assessment (LCA) in accordance with ISO 14044, focusing for the moment on the impact of inference (i.e., the use of models to answer queries) and the manufacturing of graphics cards (resource extraction, manufacturing and transport).
descs.3: The model's power consumption is estimated by taking into account various parameters such as the size and architecture of the AI model used, the location of the servers where the models are deployed, and the number of output tokens. The calculation of the global warming potential indicator, expressed in CO2 equivalent, is derived from the measurement of the model's power consumption.
descs.4: It is important to note that methodologies for assessing the environmental impact of AI are still under development.

3.title: How is the energy impact of the models calculated?

desc.1: Since 2024, thousands of users have used the arena to compare the responses of different models, generating hundreds of thousands of votes. Simply counting the number of wins is not enough to establish a ranking. A fair system must be statistically robust, adjust after each matchup, and truly reflect the value of the performances achieved.
desc.2: It is with this in mind that a ranking based on the Bradley-Terry model was established, developed in collaboration with the French Center of expertise for digital platform regulation (PEReN) teams, based on all the votes and reactions collected on the platform. To learn more, see our methodological notebook.

desc.1: The Bradley-Terry model transforms a set of local and potentially incomplete comparisons into a consistent and statistically robust global ranking system, where the empirical win rate remains limited to direct observations.

elo.title: Top 10 models in the ranking based on estimated win rate with the Bradley-Terry model

impacts.title: Impact of methodological choice on model ranking

desc.1: Based solely on the average win rate , an overall ranking can be obtained, but this calculation assumes that each model has played against all others.
desc.2: This method is not ideal because it requires data from all combinations of models and as soon as the number of models increases, it quickly becomes expensive and cumbersome to maintain.

winrate.title: Top 10 models in the ranking based on "empirical" win rates

elo.def: Definition: Ranking system where the gain or loss of points depends on the result (victory/defeat/draw and the estimated level of the opponent: if a weaker model beats a stronger model, its progression in the ranking is greater.

list.1: Probabilistic model: we can estimate the probable outcome of any matchup, even between models that have never been directly competed.
list.2: Taking match difficulty into account :The scores estimated from the Bradley Terry model take into account the level of the opponents encountered, allowing for a fair comparison between models.
list.3: Better Uncertainty Management:The confidence interval integrates the entire network of comparisons. This allows for a more accurate estimation of uncertainty, especially for models with few direct confrontations but many common opponents.

elo.title: Bradley-Terry (BT) leaderboard

winrate.def: Definition : An empirical ranking system for models based on the percentage of duels won by a model against all other models.

list.1: Game Count Bias A model that has won three out of three duels has a 100% win rate, but this score is not very meaningful because it is based on very little data.
list.2: No consideration of duel difficulty : beating a “beginner” or an “expert” model counts the same. Win rates are unfair since they do not take match difficulty into account.
list.3: Stagnation : In the long run, many good models end up around 50% win rate because they are facing models of their own skill level, which makes the rankings less discriminating.

winrate.title: Ranking by win rate

choices.both_bad: Both bad: 0 points to each model — your dissatisfaction counts, not only your relative preference.
choices.idk: I don't know: excluded from the count, it does not count for either model.

desc.1: Bradley-Terry needs a connected network of comparisons: your votes are mostly scattered, disconnected pairs, so the method does not apply at the scale of a single account. The personal score is a shrunk win rate:
desc.2: points is your point total on the model, battles the number of scored comparisons involving it, and m your average points per comparison across every model. Shrinkage pulls a rarely compared model toward that average: a single win shows 0.667 rather than 100%, and a model compared twenty times outranks one compared once at a comparable rate.

personal.title: The personal ranking: how your score is worked out

coef.footnote: Length and markdown markers are correlated: these coefficients should be read together, not as independent effects taken in isolation.
coef.hint: Regression coefficients estimated over all votes. A positive value means that this presentation dimension is associated with a higher probability of winning once the strength of the model is taken into account. That is exactly the share style control removes from the ranking.
coef.title: Measured effect of presentation

desc.1: A model can climb the ranking simply by answering at greater length or with richer formatting (headings, bold, lists), without being more relevant on substance. Style control, inspired by LMArena's “Style Control”, removes this effect: a logistic regression separates, in each vote, what comes from the strength of the model from what comes from its presentation.
desc.2: The displayed score then becomes a “style-debiased” Elo: the ranking you would get if the two compared answers were formatted in the same way. Style control is on by default; the “Style control” button at the top of the table switches back to the raw Bradley-Terry ranking for comparison.

tooltips.arch: The architecture of an LLM model refers to the design principles that define how the components of a neural network are arranged and interact to transform input data into predictive outputs, including the activation mode of parameters (dense vs. sparse), the specialization of components, and the information processing mechanisms (transformers, convolutional networks, hybrid architectures).
tooltips.consumption: Measured in watt-hours, energy consumption represents the electricity used by the model to process a request and generate the corresponding response. Model energy consumption depends on the model's size and architecture. We have chosen to display proprietary models for which we do not have transparent information about their size and architecture in gray as "unanalyzed" (N/A).
tooltips.elo: Estimated statistical score based on the Bradley-Terry model, reflecting the probability that one model is preferred over another. This score is calculated from all user votes and reactions. For more information, visit the methodology tab.

tooltips.trust_range: Interval indicating the reliability of the rank: the narrower the interval, the more reliable the rank estimate. There is a 95% chance that the model's true rank is within this range.

showRanks.help: Shows each model's exact position, from 1 to last. Two neighbouring ranks can almost never be told apart: the gap between 4th and 7th usually comes down to which votes happened to be cast. The classes say what the data supports.
